nail.e: From Middle English nail, nayl, Old English næġl, from Proto-West Germanic *nagl, from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ- (“nail”).
nail.g: The horny plate or appendage at the ends of the digits of various animals, including most reptiles, birds, and mammals (both nonhuman and hu

nail.e: From Middle English naylen, from Old English næġlan.
nail.g: To fix (an object) to another object using a nail.

naive.e: Borrowed from French naïve, feminine form of naïf, from Latin nātīvus (“native, natural”).
naive.g: Lacking worldly experience, wisdom, or judgement; unsophisticated.

naked.e: From Middle English naked, from Old English nacod, from Proto-West Germanic *nak(k)wad, from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *negʷ- (“naked”).

nakedness.e: From Middle English nakednesse, from Old English nacodnes (“nakedness”); equivalent to naked + -ness.
nakedness.g: The state or condition of being naked; nudity; bareness; defenselessness; undisguisedness.

name.e: From Middle English name, nome, from Old English nama, noma, from Proto-West Germanic *namō, from Proto-Germanic *namô (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (“name”).
name.g: Any nounal word or phrase which indicates a particular person, place, class, or thing.

name.e: From Middle English namen, from Old English namian (“to name, mention”) and ġenamian (“to name, call, appoint”), from Proto-West Germanic *namōn (“to name”).

nameless.e: From Middle English nameles, equivalent to name + -less.

namely.e: From Middle English namely, nameliche, namelike, equivalent to name + -ly.
From Middle English namely, namly, equivalent to name + -ly.

namesake.e: From the phrase “for (one's) name's sake”, first found in Bible translations as a rendering of a Calque of Hebrew לְמַעַן שְׁמוֹ (l'má'an sh'mó) idiom meaning “to protect one's reputation” or possibly “vouched for by one's reputation”. A familiar example is in Psalm 23:3.
namesake.g: An entity that lends its name to another entity.

nap.e: From Middle English nappen, from Old English hnappian (“to doze, slumber, sleep”), from Proto-West Germanic *hnappōn (“to nap”).
nap.g: To have a nap; to sleep for a short period of time, especially during the day.

nap.e: Probably of North Germanic origin, from Old Swedish nappa (“to pluck, pinch”).

napkin.e: From Middle English napekyn, napkyn, equivalent to nape (“cloth”) + -kin (diminutive suffix).
napkin.g: A serviette; a (usually rectangular) piece of cloth or paper used at the table for wiping the mouth and hands for cleanliness while eating.

nard.e: From Middle English narde, from Old French narde, Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos), from Phoenician, Sanskrit नलद (nálada, “Indian narde”).
nard.g: A flowering plant of species Nardostachys jatamansi, in the valerian family, that grows in the Himalayas and is used as a perfume, an incens

narrow.e: From Middle English narow, narowe, narewe, narwe, naru, from Old English nearu (“narrow, strait, confined, constricted, not spacious, limited, petty; limited, poor, restricted; oppressive, causing anxiety (of that which restricts free action of body or mind), causing or accompanied by difficulty, hardship, oppressive; oppressed, not having free action.
narrow.g: Having a small width; not wide; having opposite edges or sides that are close, especially by comparison to length or depth.
To reduce in width or extent; to contract.

narrowly.e: From Middle English narowly, equivalent to narrow + -ly.
narrowly.g: In a narrow manner; without flexibility or latitude.

nation.e: From Middle English nacioun, nacion, from Old French nacion, from Latin nātiōnem, accusative of nātiō (“nation”).
nation.g: A historically constituted, stable community of people, formed based on a common economic life, ethnicity, language, religion, and/or territ

native.e: From Middle English natif, from Old French natif, from Latin nātīvus, from nātus (“birth”). By surface analysis, Latin nat- + -ive.
native.g: Belonging to one by birth or ancestry.

native-born.g: Being a native and inhabitant of the same place; living where one was born.

nativity.e: From Middle English nativite, from Anglo-Norman nativite, Middle French nativite, and their source, Latin nātīvitās (“birth”). By surface analysis, native + -ity.
nativity.g: Someone's birth; the place, time and circumstances of a birth.

natural.e: From Middle English natural, borrowed from Old French natural, naturel, from Latin nātūrālis, from nātus, the perfect participle of nāscor (“be born”, verb). By surface analysis, natur(e) + -al.

naturally.e: From Middle English naturally, naturaly, naturely, naturaliche, natureliche, equivalent to natural + -ly.

nature.e: From Middle English nature, natur, from Old French nature, from Latin nātūra (“birth, origin, natural constitution or quality”), future participle from perfect passive participle (g)natus (“born”), from deponent verb (g)nasci (“to be born, originate”) + future participle suffix -urus.
nature.g: The way things are, the totality of all things in the physical universe and their order, especially the physical world in contrast to spirit

naught.e: From the Middle English naught, nought, naht, nawiht, from Old English nawiht. Equivalent to ne + aught.

naughty.e: From late Middle English noughti, naughty (“evil, immoral, wicked”), from nought (“evil, immoral”) + -ī̆ (suffix forming adjectives). Analysable as naught + -y.
naughty.g: Mischievous; tending to misbehave or act badly (especially of a child).

nauseous.e: From Latin nauseōsus (“causing nausea”), corresponding synchronically to nausea + -ous.

nave.e: Ultimately from Latin nāvem, singular accusative of nāvis, possibly via a Romance source.
nave.g: The middle or body of a church, extending from the transepts to the principal entrances.

nave.e: From Middle English nave, from Old English nafu, from Proto-West Germanic *nabu, from Proto-Germanic *nabō (compare Dutch naaf, German Nabe, Swedish nav), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nebʰ- (“navel, hub”) (compare Latin umbō (“shield boss”), Latvian naba, Sanskrit नभ्य (nabhya)).

navel.e: From Middle English navel, navele, from Old English nafola, from Proto-West Germanic *nabulō, from Proto-Germanic *nabalô (“navel”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nóbʰōl (“navel”), diminutive of *h₃nebʰ- (“hub; navel”).
navel.g: The indentation or bump remaining in the abdomen of placental mammals where the umbilical cord was attached before birth.

navy.e: From Middle English nave, navye, from Anglo-Norman, Old French navie, from Latin nāvigia < nāvigium, from Latin nāvigō, nāvis (“boat”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. By surface analysis, Latin nav- + -y.
navy.g: A country's entire maritime military force, including ships and personnel.

nay.e: From Middle English nai, nei, from Old Norse nei (“no”), contraction of ne (“not”) + ei (“ever”), itself from Proto-Germanic *nai (“never”), *nē (“not”).
